title: Definition
body_md:
We will call $\{{\mathbf X}({t}): {t\in T}\}$ a  $q$-Gaussian (non-commutative) process indexed by $T$
if
 there are vectors $h(t)\in {\mathcal H}$ such that ${\mathbf X}(t)={\mathbf X}_{h(t)}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{psi-conditionals} If ${\mathbf Y}=\psi(g_1\otimes\dots \otimes g_m)$,
${\mathbf X}_1={\mathbf X}_{f_1},\dots,{\mathbf X}_k={\mathbf X}_{f_k}$ for some $f_i,g_j\in{\mathcal H}$ and
$P:{\mathcal H}\to {\mathcal H}$ denotes orthogonal projection onto the span of $f_1,\dots,f_k$ then
$$
{\mathbb E}({\mathbf Y}|{\mathbf X}_1,\dots,{\mathbf X}_k)=\psi(Pg_1\otimes\dots\otimes P g_m).
$$

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from Theorem \ref{psi-conditionals} and (\ref{Wick-def}).
Write the orthogonal projection of $f_0$ onto the span of $f_1,\dots f_k$
as the linear combination $g=\sum_ja_j f_j$. Then
${\mathbb E}({\mathbf X}_0|{\mathbf X}_1,\dots,{\mathbf X}_k)=E(\psi(f_0)|{\mathbf X}_1,\dots,{\mathbf X}_k)=\psi(g)=\sum_j a_j\psi(f_j)$,
which proves (\ref{LR}). Similarly,
$
{\mathbb E}({\mathbf X}_0^2-\|f_0\|^2{\mathbf I}|{\mathbf X}_1,\dots,{\mathbf X}_k)={\mathbb E}(\psi(f_0\otimes f_0)|{\mathbf X}_1,\dots,{\mathbf X}_k)=
\psi(g\otimes g)=(\sum_j a_j{\mathbf X}_j)^2-\|g\|^2{\mathbf I}$.
This proves (\ref{QV}) with $c=\|f_0\|^2-\|g\|^2$.

If $f_1\dots,f_k\in{\mathcal H}$ are linearly independent then the representation
 $g=\sum_ja_j f_j$ is unique.

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{CV-def} A classical version of the process ${\mathbf X}(t)$ indexed by
${t\in T\subset {\mathbb R}}$
is a stochastic process $\tilde{X}(t)$ defined on some classical probability space such that for
any finite number of indexes $t_1<t_2<\dots<t_k$ and any polynomials
$P_1,\dots,P_k$,
\begin{eqnarray}\label{C-ver}
{\mathbb E}\left(P_1({\mathbf X}(t_1))P_2({\mathbf X}(t_2))\dots P_k({\mathbf X}(t_k))\right)=
\\ \nonumber
E\left(P_1(\tilde{X}(t_1))P_2(\tilde{X}(t_2))\dots P_k(\tilde{X}(t_k))\right).
\end{eqnarray}

title: Proof of Theorem \protect\refq-reg classic
body_md:
Since $\tilde{X},\tilde{Y},\tilde{Z}$ are bounded random variables, to prove (\ref{LR-c}) we need only to verify
that for arbitrary polynomials $P,Q$,
$$
E\left(P(\tilde{X})\tilde{Y} Q(\tilde{Z})\right)=E\left(P (\tilde{X})(a\tilde{X}+b\tilde{Z}) Q (\tilde{Z})\right).$$

 This is equivalent to
                            
$${\mathbb E}\left(P({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Y} Q({\mathbf Z})\right)={\mathbb E}\left(P ({\mathbf X})(a{\mathbf X}+b{\mathbf Z}) Q ({\mathbf Z})\right),
$$
               
see  (\ref{C-ver}).
The latter follows from (\ref{LR3}) and (\ref{E nc}),  proving (\ref{LR-c}).
               

To prove (\ref{QV-c}), we  verify
that for arbitrary polynomials $P,Q$ we have

$$E\left(P(\tilde{X})\tilde{Y}^2 Q(\tilde{Z})\right)=E\left(P (\tilde{X})(A\tilde{X}^2+B\tilde{X}\tilde{Z}+C\tilde{Z}^2+D) Q (\tilde{Z})\right).$$

By definition  (\ref{C-ver}), this is equivalent to

\begin{equation}\label{QV-nc}
{\mathbb E}\left(P({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Y}^2 Q({\mathbf Z})\right)={\mathbb E}\left(P ({\mathbf X})(A{\mathbf X}^2+B{\mathbf X}{\mathbf Z}+C{\mathbf Z}^2+D) Q ({\mathbf Z})\right).
\end{equation}
It suffices to show that (\ref{QV-nc}) holds true when
$P=H_n$ and $Q=H_m$ are the $q$-Hermite polynomials defined by (\ref{q-H}).
Formula (\ref{QV3}) implies that the left-hand side of (\ref{QV-nc}) is given by
$$ c{\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X})H_m({\mathbf Z}))+
a^2{\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}^2H_m({\mathbf Z}))+b^2 {\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}^2H_m({\mathbf Z}))$$
$$
+ab {\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}{\mathbf Z} H_m({\mathbf Z}))+ab {\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}{\mathbf X} H_m({\mathbf Z})),
$$
and the right-hand side becomes
$$
A{\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}^2H_m({\mathbf Z}))+C {\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}^2H_m({\mathbf Z}))
+$$
$$B {\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}{\mathbf Z} H_m({\mathbf Z}))+ D{\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X})H_m({\mathbf Z})).
$$
Using formulas from Lemma \ref{switch} we can see that both sides are zero, except when $m=n$
or $m=n\pm 2$. We now consider these three cases separately.

\noindent
{\it Case $m=n+2$}:
Using Lemma \ref{switch},  (\ref{QV-nc}) simplifies to
$$
(a^2\langle f, h \rangle^2+2ab \langle f, h \rangle+b^2)\langle f, h \rangle^n[n+2]_q!=(A\langle f, h \rangle^2+B\langle f, h \rangle+C)\langle f, h \rangle^n[n+2]_q!.
$$
This equation is satisfied when   coefficients $A,B,C$ satisfy the equation
\begin{equation}\label{ABC 1}
A\langle f, h \rangle^2+B\langle f, h \rangle+C=a^2\langle f, h \rangle^2+2ab \langle f, h \rangle+b^2.
\end{equation}

\noindent
{\it Case $m=n-2$}:
Using Lemma \ref{switch},  (\ref{QV-nc}) simplifies to
$$
(a^2+2ab \langle f, h \rangle+b^2\langle f, h \rangle^2)\langle f, h \rangle^{n-2}[n]_q!=(A+B\langle f, h \rangle+C\langle f, h \rangle^2)\langle f, h \rangle^{n-2}[n]_q!.
$$
This equation is satisfied whenever
\begin{equation}\label{ABC 2}
A+B\langle f, h \rangle+C\langle f, h \rangle^2=a^2+2ab \langle f, h \rangle+b^2\langle f, h \rangle^2.
\end{equation}

\noindent {\it Case $m=n$}:                                            
We use again Lemma \ref{switch}.
On both sides of Eq. (\ref{QV-nc}) we factor out
$\langle f, h \rangle^{n-1}[n]_q!$, and equate the remaining coefficients.
(This is allowed since we are after sufficient conditions only!)
We get
$$
\left(\langle f, h \rangle (a^2+b^2)([n+1]_q+[n]_q)+ab \left(\langle f, h \rangle^2[n+1]_q+
(1+q)[n]_q\right)+c\langle f, h \rangle
\right)
=$$
$$
\left((1+q)(A+C)+B(q\langle f, h \rangle^2+1)[n]_q+D\langle f, h \rangle\right).
$$
Now we use $[n+1]_q=1+q[n]_q$. Suppressing the correction to
the constant term (i.e., the term free of $n$),
we get

$$
(1+q)\left(\langle f, h \rangle (a^2+b^2)+ab(1+\langle f, h \rangle^2)\right)[n]_q+c\langle f, h \rangle+\dots
=$$

$$
\left((1+q)(A+C)\langle f, h \rangle+B(q\langle f, h \rangle^2+1)\right)
[n]_q+D\langle f, h \rangle,
$$
where $c+\dots$  denotes the suppressed constant term corrections.

This equation holds true when  the coefficients at $[n]_q$ match, which gives
\begin{equation}\label{ABC 3}
(1+q)\langle f, h \rangle(A+C)+B(q\langle f, h \rangle^2+1)=(1+q)\left((a^2+b^2)\langle f, h \rangle+ab(\langle f, h \rangle^2+1)\right),
\end{equation}
and the constant terms match: $c+\dots=D$. The latter holds true
 when the expectations are equal  ($n=m=0$), and hence this condition
is equivalent to
(\ref{D}). The remaining three equations  (\ref{ABC 1}), (\ref{ABC 2}), and (\ref{ABC 3}) have
a unique solution given by the expressions (\ref{A}), (\ref{B}), (\ref{C}).

title: Proof of Lemma \protect\refswitch
body_md:
Using the definition of vacuum expectation state,
(\ref{Wick-appl}) and (\ref{psi-Hermit}) we get
${\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}{\mathbf X} H_m({\mathbf Z}))=
\langle {\mathbf Z} H_n({\mathbf X})\Phi |{\mathbf X} H_m({\mathbf Z})\Phi \rangle_q=
\langle {\mathbf X}_h f^{\otimes n}|{\mathbf X}_f h^{\otimes m}\rangle_q$.
Therefore (\ref{anihilate}), and (\ref{create})   imply

\begin{eqnarray}\label{foo*}
&&{\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}{\mathbf X} H_m({\mathbf Z}))= \\
&&\langle [n]_q\langle f, h \rangle f^{\otimes n-1}+h\otimes  f^{\otimes n}|
 [m]_q\langle f, h \rangle h^{\otimes m-1}+f\otimes  h^{\otimes m}
\rangle_q .\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
The latter is zero, except when $m=n$ or $m=n\pm 2$.
We will consider these two cases separately.

If $m=n$, by orthogonality  we have
$${\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}{\mathbf X} H_m({\mathbf Z}))=
[n]_q^2\langle f, h \rangle^2
\langle f^{\otimes n-1}| h^{\otimes n-1}
\rangle_q
+
\langle h\otimes  f^{\otimes n}|f\otimes  h^{\otimes n}
\rangle_q.
$$
Clearly, $\langle f^{\otimes n-1}| h^{\otimes n-1}
\rangle_q =\langle f, h \rangle^{n-1}[n-1]_q!$; this can be seen either from (\ref{H-norm nc}) and (\ref{E(H|X)}),
or directly from the definition (\ref{q-scalar}).

By (\ref{q-scalar}) the second term splits into the sum over permutations
$\sigma'\in S_{n+1}$ such that $\sigma'(1)=1$ and the sum over the permutations such that
$\sigma'(1)=k>1$. This gives

$$\langle h\otimes  f^{\otimes n}|f\otimes  h^{\otimes n}
\rangle_q=
\sum_{\sigma\in S_n} \langle f, h \rangle q^{|\sigma|}\langle f, h \rangle^n
+\sum_{k=2}^{n+1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}q^{k-1+|\sigma|}\langle f, h \rangle^{n-1}
=$$
$$\langle f, h \rangle^{n+1}[n]_q!+\langle f, h \rangle^{n-1}q[n]_q [n]_q!.
$$
Elementary algebra now yields (\ref{H(X)ZXH(Z)}) for $m=n$.
                                                                                     


If $m=n+2$, then the right-hand side of (\ref{foo*}) consists of only one term
we get
$${\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf Z}{\mathbf X} H_{n+2}({\mathbf Z}))=
 [n+2]_q\langle f, h \rangle \langle h\otimes f^{\otimes n}| h^{\otimes n+1}
\rangle_q=$$
$$ [n+2]_q\langle f, h \rangle \sum_{\sigma\in S_{n+1}} q^{|\sigma|}\langle f, h \rangle^n=\langle f, h \rangle^{n+1}[n+2]_q!.
$$

Since $m=n-2$ is given by the same expression with the roles of $m,n$ switched around, this ends the proof of (\ref{H(X)ZXH(Z)}).


The remaining expectations match the corresponding commutative values,
 and can also be  evaluated using  recurrence (\ref{q-H}) and formulas (\ref{E(H|X)}), and
(\ref{H-norm nc}).


To prove (\ref{H(X)XZH(Z)}) notice that
since ${\mathbf X}$ and $H_n({\mathbf X})$ commute, using (\ref{q-H}) and (\ref{E(H|X)}) we get
$${\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}{\mathbf Z} H_m({\mathbf Z}))={\mathbb E}({\mathbf X} H_n({\mathbf X})(H_{m+1}({\mathbf Z})+[m]_qH_{m-1}({\mathbf Z})))
=$$
$$
\langle f, h \rangle^{m+1}{\mathbb E}({\mathbf X} H_n({\mathbf X})H_{m+1}({\mathbf X}))+ [m]_q\langle f, h \rangle^{m-1}{\mathbb E}({\mathbf X} H_n({\mathbf X})H_{m-1}({\mathbf X})).
$$
The only non-zero values are when $m=n$, or $m=n\pm 2$. Using (\ref{q-H}) again, and then
 (\ref{H-norm nc})
we get (\ref{H(X)XZH(Z)}).

              
                                                                                          
    
                                                                                    
                                  
   
                                                                                               
   
                                                                          
                                                                                  
                                                           
                                                                                      

                                     
                                    
                                 
                                                                          
 
Since  by (\ref{E(H|X)}) we have
$${\mathbb E}(H_n({\mathbf X}){\mathbf X}^2 H_m({\mathbf Z}))=\langle f, h \rangle^m {\mathbb E}{\mathbf X}^2 H_n({\mathbf X})H_m({\mathbf X}),$$
recurrence (\ref{q-H}) used twice proves (\ref{H(X)X2H(Z)}).

Formula (\ref{L2}) is an immediate consequence of (\ref{E(H|X)}) and (\ref{H-norm nc}).

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the case $q=-1$ is well known, we restrict our attention to the case
 $-1<q<1$.
Our starting point is expression (\ref{QV-c}).
A computation shows that
 the conditional variance $Var(\tilde{Y}|\tilde{X},\tilde{Z}):=E(\tilde{Y}^2|\tilde{X},\tilde{Z})-\left(E(\tilde{Y}|\tilde{X},\tilde{Z})\right)^2$ is as follows.
\begin{eqnarray} \label{foo1}
Var(\tilde{Y}|\tilde{X},\tilde{Z})=&1-a^2-b^2-
ab\langle f, h \rangle \frac{(1+q)(1-\langle f, h \rangle^2)+2(1-q)}{1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2}
-&\\ \nonumber
&\frac {ab\left(1-q\right)}
{1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2}\left(\tilde{Z}{\langle f, h \rangle-\tilde{X}}\right )\left ({\langle f, h \rangle}\tilde{X}-\tilde{Z}\right).
&
\end{eqnarray}
The right-hand side of this expression must be non-negative over the support of $\tilde{X},\tilde{Z}$.
It is known, see  \cite[Lemma
8.1]{Bryc98} or \cite[Theorem 1.10]{BKS97}, that $\tilde{X},\tilde{Z}$ have the joint
probability density function $f(x,z)$ with respect to the product of marginals $\nu_q$.
Moreover, $f$ is
 defined for all $-2/\sqrt{1-q}\leq x,z\leq 2/\sqrt{1-q}$ and from
its explicit product expansion we can see that
 $$f(x,z)\geq \prod_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(1-\langle f, h \rangle^2 q^k)}{
(1+\langle f, h \rangle q^{k})^4}$$
 is  strictly positive. In particular, the right-hand side of (\ref{foo1}) must be non-negative
when evaluated at $\tilde{X}=\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{1-q},\tilde{Z}=-\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{1-q}$.


Using formulas (\ref{a}), (\ref{b}) with the above values of $\tilde{X},\tilde{Y}$
we get the rational expression for the conditional variance which can be written as follows.
\begin{eqnarray} \label{foo2}
&\left(1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2\right)\left(1-\langle f, h \rangle\right)^2Var\left(\tilde{Y}|\tilde{X},\tilde{Z}\right)=& \\ \nonumber
&
(1-\langle f, h \rangle)^2\left(1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2+(1+q)\langle f, h \rangle\langle f, g \rangle\langle g, h \rangle\right)-&
\\ \nonumber &\left(\langle f, g \rangle-\langle g, h \rangle\right)^2(1+\langle f, h \rangle^2) .
&
\end{eqnarray}
Therefore
$$(1-\langle f, h \rangle)^2\left(1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2+(1+q)\langle f, h \rangle\langle f, g \rangle\langle g, h \rangle\right)
\geq $$
$$\left(\langle f, g \rangle-\langle g, h \rangle\right)^2(1+\langle f, h \rangle^2).$$

Since the assumptions imply that $1-q\langle f, h \rangle^2+(1+q)\langle f, h \rangle\langle f, g \rangle\langle g, h \rangle\leq 1+\langle f, h \rangle^2$, this implies
$(1-\langle f, h \rangle)^2 \geq \left(\langle f, g \rangle-\langle g, h \rangle\right)^2$, proving (\ref{Bell}).

title: Example
body_md:
\label{E1} Consider the case $\langle f, h \rangle=\langle g, h \rangle>0$. This can be realized when  the
covariance matrix is non-negative definite; a computation shows that this is equivalent
to the condition $2\langle f, h \rangle^2\leq 1+\langle f, g \rangle$. Since (\ref{sub-M}) is satisfied, Bell's inequality (\ref{Bell})
implies $1+\langle f, g \rangle\geq 2\langle f, h \rangle$. Therefore, all choices of vectors $f,g,h\in{\mathcal H}$
such that
$
\langle f, h \rangle=\langle g, h \rangle$, $0<\langle f, h \rangle<1$, and $2\langle f, h \rangle^2-1<\langle f, g \rangle<2\langle f, h \rangle-1$
lead to $q$-Gaussian triplets with no classical version for $-1\leq q<1$.
